# Reconstruction of the 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive assessment

The strongest public evidence supports the following reconstruction: the 2023 3CX DesktopApp compromise began when a 3CX employee’s computer was infected through a previously compromised Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer. The attackers used that foothold to move through 3CX’s corporate environment, compromise both Windows and macOS build infrastructure, and insert malicious code into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers. The trojanized installers were then distributed to 3CX customers, creating a cascading software supply-chain compromise. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The activity was publicly associated with a North Korea-linked threat ecosystem. Mandiant tracked the operation as **UNC4736**, assessed it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, and connected it with financially motivated “AppleJeus” activity with moderate confidence. Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram-related activity to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence, while other reporting used labels including **Labyrinth Chollima**, **Kimsuky**, **Emerald Sleet**, or **Velvet Chollima**. These names should not be treated as proven interchangeable identities. The most defensible conclusion is that the compromise was publicly attributed to a North Korea-linked cluster associated with Lazarus/AppleJeus activity, but that the precise organizational identity and sub-group attribution remained uncertain. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

The campaign’s apparent operational objective was selective follow-on access to high-value organizations, especially cryptocurrency and financial-technology companies. The available evidence demonstrates targeted deployment of the Gopuram backdoor to fewer than ten observed machines, but it does not establish that cryptocurrency theft was successfully completed. ([S2](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

## Sources and evidentiary basis

For clarity, this report uses the following source identifiers:

| ID | Source | Primary evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Cybersecurity Dive, March 30, 2023 | Initial public reporting, affected versions and scale |
| S2 | WIRED, April 3, 2023 | Gopuram deployment and selective cryptocurrency targeting |
| S3 | Mandiant/Google Cloud, April 20, 2023 | Technical reconstruction and initial intrusion vector |
| S4 | Kaspersky Securelist, April 3, 2023 | Gopuram analysis and Lazarus attribution |
| S5 | Google TAG, March 24, 2022 | Earlier AppleJeus activity and Trading Technologies infrastructure compromise |
| S6 | MITRE ATT&CK, AppleJeus S0584 | AppleJeus malware profile and Lazarus association |
| S7 | MITRE ATT&CK, Lazarus Group G0032 | Lazarus aliases, techniques, and attribution context |
| S8 | WIRED, April 20, 2023 | Public explanation of the cascading supply-chain model |
| S9 | Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, March 31, 2023 | Affected 3CX versions and defensive guidance |

## What was compromised and how broadly

3CX DesktopApp was enterprise communications software supporting voice calls, video conferencing, chat, and related functions. The application was used by more than 600,000 corporate customers and reportedly had more than 12 million daily active users. Huntress reported that Shodan data showed more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems, while it had issued 2,595 incident reports involving a maliciously signed `3CXDesktopApp.exe` binary. These figures describe potential exposure and observed indicators, not confirmed compromise of every organization. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency identified affected Windows Electron versions **18.12.407** and **18.12.416**, and affected macOS Electron versions **18.11.1213**, **18.12.402**, **18.12.407**, and **18.12.416**. The agency stated that the trojanized application could harvest system information and steal data and stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. ([S9](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/))

The initial malicious activity was observed in late March 2023. CrowdStrike reported unexpected behavior from a legitimate, signed binary, including beaconing to attacker-controlled infrastructure, deployment of second-stage payloads, and, in a small number of cases, hands-on-keyboard activity. The public reporting initially focused on Windows; the state of macOS activity was less certain among researchers at that stage. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/))

## Reconstruction of the intrusion chain

### Stage 1: Prior compromise of Trading Technologies software

Mandiant’s investigation identified the initial compromise of 3CX’s network as a malicious software package downloaded from the Trading Technologies website. Specifically, Mandiant identified a tampered installer named `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`, with MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`. The installer was associated with the X_TRADER trading application, which Trading Technologies had reportedly discontinued in 2020 but continued to make available for download through 2022. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The compromised X_TRADER installer was digitally signed with a certificate whose subject was “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” It contained a signed `Setup.exe`, which dropped malicious DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to side-load one of the malicious DLLs. The malicious components then used **SIGFLIP** and **DAVESHELL** to decrypt and load a modular backdoor named **VEILEDSIGNAL**. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The evidence therefore indicates that the 3CX intrusion did not begin with an attacker directly compromising the 3CX build server. Instead, the first identified access path was a compromised third-party software package used on a 3CX employee’s computer. WIRED reported that the employee’s machine was infected through the X_TRADER supply-chain compromise, after which the attackers moved into the 3CX network. ([S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

The exact method by which Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER package was originally altered remains unresolved in the supplied evidence. Mandiant had not been hired by Trading Technologies to investigate that earlier compromise, and therefore could not establish how the original tampering occurred or how many other X_TRADER users may have been affected. ([S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

### Stage 2: Establishment of access inside 3CX

Once the compromised X_TRADER software infected the 3CX employee’s computer, the attackers used the resulting access to move laterally through the 3CX environment. Mandiant reported credential harvesting and lateral movement inside the organization. The attackers ultimately compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

On the Windows build environment, Mandiant identified a compiled version of the open-source **Fast Reverse Proxy** project. The file was named `MsMpEng.exe`, was placed in `C:\Windows\System32`, and had MD5 hash `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`. Mandiant assessed that this tool was used to facilitate movement within the 3CX organization. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The attackers also deployed the **TAXHAUL** launcher and **COLDCAT** downloader on the Windows build environment. TAXHAUL persisted through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service and operated with LocalSystem privileges. COLDCAT generated host identifiers and communicated with command-and-control infrastructure, receiving shellcode after an initial handshake. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

On the macOS build server, Mandiant identified the **POOLRAT** backdoor using Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described in reporting as a new malware family was, in its assessment, POOLRAT. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Stage 3: Compromise of the 3CX build process

The attackers’ access to the build environment enabled them to compromise the software-production process rather than merely infect individual 3CX endpoints. Mandiant reported that the Windows and macOS build environments were both compromised. The resulting malicious changes were incorporated into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers distributed through the company’s normal update and download channels. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Mandiant described this as the first instance it had identified in which one software supply-chain compromise directly led to another software supply-chain compromise. The sequence was therefore:

1. Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software was compromised.
2. A 3CX employee installed or used the compromised X_TRADER package.
3. Attackers obtained access to the 3CX corporate environment.
4. The attackers moved laterally and harvested credentials.
5. The Windows and macOS build environments were compromised.
6. Malicious code was inserted into 3CX DesktopApp installers.
7. The trojanized 3CX software was distributed to downstream customers. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

### Stage 4: Trojanized customer software and first-stage payloads

The affected 3CX DesktopApp versions contained malicious code that ran a downloader identified by Mandiant as **SUDDENICON**. SUDDENICON retrieved additional command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. The next identified stage was **ICONICSTEALER**, a data-mining component capable of collecting browser information and application configuration data. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

Kaspersky described a related execution sequence in which the infected MSI installer contained a modified DLL that decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`. The decrypted payload extracted command-and-control URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository, connected to a command-and-control server, and downloaded an infostealer. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

The use of legitimate signing and DLL side-loading made the software appear trustworthy and helped the malicious activity evade routine user suspicion. Sophos’s DLL-sideloading observation was reported in the early coverage, while Mandiant documented the more extensive loading process and its relationship to the earlier X_TRADER compromise. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

## Follow-on targeting and Gopuram

The 3CX compromise functioned as a broad initial-access mechanism, but the evidence indicates that the attackers did not deploy their most capable payload to every infected customer. Kaspersky observed the **Gopuram** backdoor on fewer than ten machines in its telemetry and reported that these systems were associated with cryptocurrency-focused companies. Kaspersky characterized this as “surgical precision.” ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Gopuram was a modular backdoor capable of connecting to command-and-control infrastructure, interacting with the victim’s file system, creating processes, and launching in-memory modules. Kaspersky documented modules for registry manipulation, service management, timestomping, process injection, network and user management, and payload updating. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

Kaspersky identified persistence involving `wlbsctrl.dll`, the IKEEXT service, and an encrypted shellcode file under:

```text
C:\Windows\System32\config\TxR\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms
```

It also reported additional DLL side-loading involving `ualapi.dll` in `spoolsv.exe` and `ncobjapi.dll` in `svchost.exe`. These findings indicate that the Gopuram phase was not merely browser-data collection; it provided a full post-compromise capability on selected hosts. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

WIRED reported that Kaspersky had not observed evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft in the systems it examined. Accordingly, cryptocurrency theft is a plausible and strongly supported objective, but not a demonstrated outcome of the specific 3CX cases described in the supplied sources. ([S2](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/))

## Public attribution

### UNC4736 and North Korean nexus

Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, describing it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Its reasoning included shared loading techniques, overlapping malware, related infrastructure, and a sustained interest in cryptocurrency and fintech targets. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

### Lazarus and AppleJeus associations

Kaspersky attributed the 3CX campaign to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. Its assessment rested on several associations: Gopuram had previously coexisted with AppleJeus on a cryptocurrency-company victim; Gopuram had been used against cryptocurrency companies; infrastructure overlapped with activity associated with AppleJeus; and domains such as `oilycargo[.]com` and `wirexpro[.]com` had previously been linked by researchers to Lazarus-related operations. ([S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/))

MITRE ATT&CK identifies AppleJeus as malware associated with Lazarus Group and describes AppleJeus as a family of downloaders initially found in trojanized cryptocurrency applications. MITRE also records Lazarus targeting finance, technology, telecommunications, government, and other sectors across multiple countries. ([S6](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/))

MITRE cautions that “Lazarus Group” is an umbrella term covering multiple North Korean cyber operators and that North Korean units may share personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft. This is important because it limits how precisely the 3CX activity can be assigned to a single operational unit. ([S7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

### Labyrinth Chollima and other naming differences

Early CrowdStrike reporting associated the activity with **Labyrinth Chollima**, a North Korea-linked group. Early WIRED reporting later used the names **Kimsuky**, **Emerald Sleet**, and **Velvet Chollima** when describing the suspected actor. These labels are not reconciled by the supplied sources and should therefore be treated as competing public naming conventions or attribution hypotheses rather than as established synonyms. ([S1](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))

The Google TAG material predates the 3CX incident and documents an AppleJeus campaign exploiting Chrome vulnerability CVE-2022-0609 against cryptocurrency and fintech organizations. TAG also identified `www.tradingtechnologies[.]com` as a compromised website in February 2022. This evidence supports the broader relationship between the 3CX activity, AppleJeus-like operations, cryptocurrency targeting, and Trading Technologies infrastructure, but it does not independently prove that the same operator performed every step of the 3CX intrusion. ([S5](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/))

## Contradictions and unresolved questions

| Issue | Evidence difference | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Exact actor name | CrowdStrike reporting used Labyrinth Chollima; WIRED cited Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, or Velvet Chollima; Mandiant used UNC4736; Kaspersky used Lazarus | North Korea-linked attribution is stronger than any single sub-group label |
| Final objective | Cryptocurrency targeting was repeatedly observed or inferred, but Kaspersky reported no observed theft | Targeting objective is supported; successful theft is unconfirmed |
| macOS activity | Early reporting said macOS activity was not consistently confirmed; CSA listed affected macOS versions and Mandiant found POOLRAT on a macOS build server | macOS was affected at least in the build environment, while endpoint-level scope was initially uncertain |
| Initial Trading Technologies compromise | Mandiant identified the compromised X_TRADER package but did not investigate how Trading Technologies itself was breached | The 3CX chain’s initial access is established; the earlier attacker entry into Trading Technologies is unresolved |
| Number of victims | 3CX reported hundreds of thousands of potential users; Kaspersky saw Gopuram on fewer than ten systems | Broad exposure and narrow second-stage targeting are both consistent with the evidence |

## Conclusion

The public evidence forms a coherent cascading compromise chain. The initiating event for the 3CX intrusion was the use of a maliciously modified X_TRADER installer obtained from the Trading Technologies website. That prior supply-chain compromise infected a 3CX employee’s machine and gave attackers access to the 3CX network. The attackers then harvested credentials, moved laterally, compromised the Windows and macOS build environments, and inserted malicious components into signed 3CX DesktopApp installers. Those installers distributed first-stage malware to customers, after which the attackers selectively deployed additional payloads, including Gopuram, against a small number of high-value targets. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise))

The most defensible public attribution is to a **North Korea-linked financially motivated activity cluster**, with the operation tracked by Mandiant as **UNC4736** and linked with moderate confidence to **AppleJeus** activity. Kaspersky’s Lazarus attribution is supported by malware, infrastructure, and victimology overlaps, but MITRE’s own description of Lazarus as an umbrella term means that the evidence does not justify claiming a uniquely identified Lazarus subgroup with certainty. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S4](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S6](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/); [S7](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/))

The principal significance of the incident is structural: it demonstrated that a compromised software supply chain can become the delivery mechanism for compromising another software vendor’s development and distribution process. The 3CX case therefore represents not simply a malicious update, but a documented supply-chain chain reaction. ([S3](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two))
